newsitem.title: UK: European Grains - A focus on quality.
newsitem.headline: European Grains - A focus on quality.

text.p: The focus in European grains this week before Friday's holiday halted activity was on quality as traders assessed the new crop.
Austria, Belgium, France, Greece, parts of Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, Poland, Portugal and Spain were among the countries which were closed on Friday.

Scattered rain disrupted the final stages of the French harvest, as well as the developing English wheat harvest in mid-week, but it was followed by clear, sunny weather, which meant that most farmers were able to restart work quickly, farming sources said.

French traders said they had seen some harvest pressure, with most of the crop now in. Quality remained an important issue for the market, although there were fewer problems with Hagberg than had been expected. However, the market was developing a split on the basis of test weight.
There was a "relatively active," market in low specific weight wheat, one trader said.
And French wheat was competitive, with traders citing interest from Italy, Spain and Portugal.

In Britain a volatile sterling had stifled trade in futures and the physical market by the end of the week. There was little sign of harvest pressure, although more wheat is likely to be coming off farms from next week, one trader said.
"With yields down, the farmer isn't going to be in too much of a rush to let go of wheat," he said.
English wheat was uncompetitive, on export markets, with sales lost to Danish competition in recent days. But there were some export deals being done in oats and barley, he said.
German grain sellers were maintaining high export prices for wheat despite a lack of immediate ex-harvest buying, traders said.
They said sellers were prepared to store the grain away and await higher autumn prices. Ample storage space is available.
Sellers were not prepared to reduce levels to accommodate domestic millers' price ideas or to lure absent eastern European consumers.
Fob Baltic offers vary between 280 and 317.50 marks/tonne, with a 5,000 tonne load of Aug/Sept 12 percent wheat at 287.50.
Wheat harvests in northern German export regions will be finished next week amid sunny weather and qualities as well as volumes look promising.
Rye, triticale and barley harvests are already complete.
Rye was mostly destined for intervention while triticale, a wheat/rye hybrid, was selling well to the compound feed industry, traders said.
Traders said the EU's allocation on Thursday of 85,000 tonnes of free market wheat exports with a tax of 0.10 Ecus/tonne was in line with expectations.
The EU would shortly reach earlier pre-harvest export targets of one million tonnes.
The Spanish grains market was thin this week ahead of the public holiday on Friday.

"There's not much going on and business is mainly local. Most of the activity we've been involved in have been sales of Portuguese wheat in Spain, which looks like a bargain at these levels," said a Madrid broker.
Barley continued to come onto the market as harvesting in the north drew to a close, dealers said.
"Specific weights for barley are a little on the low side while humidity is around 13 percent, versus an average of about 11 or 10 percent in previous years," said one trader.
Durum wheat prices remain high despite poor quality because demand from Italy is still strong, he added.
Maize meanwhile continues to develop well.

"The crop is in good condition, and buyers are waiting for harvesting to start as they think there'll be more than anticipated originally. Prices should start to move down soon," said the Madrid broker.
Maize harvesting should start in the southern region of Andalusia at the end of August, he added. The bulk of Spain's crop comes from the north, and is due for harvest in September.
